When the pandemic began reshaping the world in early 2020, Sarah Riley was helping guide finance at Zoom through an unprecedented surge in demand. “You could see the volume of Zoom almost spiking up by the regions that were going into shutdown,” Riley tells us. What followed was unlike anything most software companies had experienced before. During her four years at Zoom, the company expanded from roughly $200 million in ARR to $4 billion, Riley tells us. At one point, Zoom spent nearly half a billion dollars on AWS infrastructure costs it had not anticipated, she explains.
Read More
For Riley, the experience fundamentally reshaped how she viewed finance leadership. Rather than becoming fixated on gross margin guidance or traditional planning cycles, she says the finance team had to continually reevaluate the “strategic heart” of the business as Zoom evolved from an enterprise software company into a platform supporting schools, consumers, and businesses worldwide. “Forecasting and discipline comes second” in moments of extraordinary change, Riley tells us.
That mindset now informs her role as CFO of dbt Labs, where she oversees finance, accounting, and data operations while helping guide the company through its merger with Fivetran. Riley says today’s defining challenge for software businesses is balancing legacy operating models with the realities of AI-driven transformation. “You need to balance that with how do we make sure that we’re investing aggressively enough in capturing what our user base is turning into,” she tells us.

CFOTL: Let’s find out about dbt Labs and this opportunity. You joined as a senior finance person, but within two years you were in the CFO office. It seems like a perfect match. Tell us about DBT first. What’s the company about today?
Riley: DBT is an open-source data infrastructure company. If you talked to our CEO when he started the company nine years ago, his ethos was really about taking software engineering best practices that make code bases organized, high velocity, and easy to govern, and bringing those principles to data teams. Historically, data teams were running these spaghetti code bases that were difficult to manage. We’ve all had the experience of getting an opaque number from a data partner and asking, “Can you help me trace this back to the source?” and finding that incredibly difficult.
Read More
When I joined dbt, the company had very little revenue — I think below $15 million in ARR — but there were already tens of thousands of companies using the open-source product. That told me the company was doing something special that really resonated with data developers. Since then, the platform has evolved into something much more robust that helps organizations govern data cross-platform at scale. In a world where CIOs and chief data officers are deeply focused on ensuring data quality doesn’t become a barrier to AI adoption, that’s become an increasingly important area of infrastructure.
CFOTL: Can we ask about the merger? I know there was a major announcement last year.
Riley: Last October, dbt signed a definitive agreement to merge with Fivetran, and we’re deeply excited about it. DBT and Fivetran have both become best-of-breed midsize players in the data platform space, and together the combined company becomes the third-largest standalone data platform company in the world behind Databricks and Snowflake.
It’s been a fascinating transaction to work on because the companies share so much common ground. Both organizations grew up at roughly the same time and both have very similar philosophies around being platform agnostic and supporting the user. It really felt like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to bring together two companies with such strong alignment.
CFOTL: Tell us something about your mindset when it comes to performance and what really drives performance in this business.
Riley: In addition to managing finance and accounting, I also manage our data team, so we spend a lot of time thinking about how to leverage our platform to create a truly data-driven environment internally. We’re very focused on product analytics, go-to-market analytics, and having absolute clarity around the KPIs that matter across every area of the business.
We invest early in building strong data literacy and accountability among our executives so that when we review financials, we’re reviewing them in tandem with business KPIs. Everyone understands that the investments we make are intended to drive specific outcomes. Every couple of quarters we revisit those assumptions to make sure we’re still focused on the right things. It’s really a hand-in-hand finance and data effort.
CFOTL: Before the results show up, what inputs matter most?
Riley: For us, the business KPIs are really the leading indicators. We focus heavily on the health and growth of our open-source community because that effectively becomes the top of our funnel. We’re constantly evaluating how customers are using new features, how that drives adoption of the platform product, and how we can make the experience even more compelling.
That thinking flows into our go-to-market planning as well. Do we have the right sellers? Do we have the right resources allocated? Do we have the right “chess pieces” on the board to hit our goals? Then we reflect back and ask whether those assumptions produced the financial profile we expected.
CFOTL: Can you share a little more about your insight into the customer experience and your efforts to understand it?
Riley: We try to be thoughtful about customer privacy, especially on the open-source side, so we don’t collect an excessive amount of data there. But we absolutely monitor feature consumption among customers who move onto the platform. We want to understand what they find valuable and what drives conversion.
For many open-source companies, the community is viewed primarily as a way to drive adoption or contribute to the engineering ecosystem. But from a finance perspective, I think you have to think about open source fundamentally as a distribution method. Our North Star is making sure that the commercial platform is valuable enough that it becomes an obvious next step for users. DBT’s open-source community is still growing about 70% year-over-year at scale, with more than 100,000 companies on the platform, so the opportunity is significant.

At a glance
 The dbt Labs team overcame scalability and data accuracy issues by transitioning from Google Sheets to Pigment.
 They needed a flexible solution that could scale effectively with a fast-changing business in a fast-changing macro environment.
 They chose Pigment, impressed by its integration and scenario analysis capabilities.
Founded in 2016, dbt Labs is a tech company based in Philadelphia and the creator of dbt (data build tool), an open-source tool that enables data analysts and engineers to manage data in their warehouses more efficiently and collaboratively.
> “I’ve done several EPM implementations over the last decade of my career, and every time we’ve had a solution that wasn’t nimble enough to meet the business needs. That’s what pushed us to Pigment. Being a data transformation company, our ethos of bringing data together really aligns to what Pigment does.”

Retiring the spreadsheet
Before Pigment, the finance team were being held back by their use of spreadsheets.
> "We were doing everything on Google Sheets, and the difficulty in managing the data flow, it fell out of being current/accurate really quickly, it was really manual, and with the pace of growth the team was experiencing, it wasn’t going to scale for our financial planning needs."
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
Why Pigment?
dbt Labs needed an effective solution that would not only accommodate their growing needs but also streamline their operations, particularly in workforce planning. Pigment stood out for the following reasons:
 Scalability: Being a growing business, dbt Labs required a tool that could grow along with it. Pigment provided a solution that removed the limitations they were experiencing with Google Sheets.
 Real-time data: One of the standout offerings of Pigment was the ability to track the progress of different teams in real-time, ensuring interventions could be made where required.
 Data accuracy: The complexities of managing multiple spreadsheets often give rise to errors. Pigment eliminated this risk with an all-in-one, automated platform.
 Scenario planning: dbt Labs needed the ability to rapidly spin up and explore business scenarios.
> “The ability to take a baseline and play through multiple different scenarios and get back to your executive teams with the implications quickly is really important. It’s an exciting time to be in finance, because we’re offering more value.”
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
The result
Before Pigment, updating Google Sheets took days of team members’ time just to analyze progress against the plan. Now, dbt Labs has seamless data flow, particularly around workforce planning. That means they’re able to check in before the end of quarter to help teams hit their goals, rather than waiting until they’re near the finish line.

1185: Scaling Smarter in the AI Era | Sarah Riley, CFO, dbt Labs
1185: Scaling Smarter in the AI Era | Sarah Riley, CFO, dbt Labs
When the pandemic began reshaping the world in early 2020, Sarah Riley was helping guide finance at Zoom through an unprecedented surge in demand. “You could see the volume of Zoom almost spiking up by the regions that were going into shutdown,” Riley tells us. What followed was unlike anything most software companies had experienced before. During her four years at Zoom, the company expanded from roughly $200 million in ARR to $4 billion, Riley tells us. At one point, Zoom spent nearly half a billion dollars on AWS infrastructure costs it had not anticipated, she explains.
Read More
For Riley, the experience fundamentally reshaped how she viewed finance leadership. Rather than becoming fixated on gross margin guidance or traditional planning cycles, she says the finance team had to continually reevaluate the “strategic heart” of the business as Zoom evolved from an enterprise software company into a platform supporting schools, consumers, and businesses worldwide. “Forecasting and discipline comes second” in moments of extraordinary change, Riley tells us.
That mindset now informs her role as CFO of dbt Labs, where she oversees finance, accounting, and data operations while helping guide the company through its merger with Fivetran. Riley says today’s defining challenge for software businesses is balancing legacy operating models with the realities of AI-driven transformation. “You need to balance that with how do we make sure that we’re investing aggressively enough in capturing what our user base is turning into,” she tells us.

CFOTL: Let’s find out about dbt Labs and this opportunity. You joined as a senior finance person, but within two years you were in the CFO office. It seems like a perfect match. Tell us about DBT first. What’s the company about today?
Riley: DBT is an open-source data infrastructure company. If you talked to our CEO when he started the company nine years ago, his ethos was really about taking software engineering best practices that make code bases organized, high velocity, and easy to govern, and bringing those principles to data teams. Historically, data teams were running these spaghetti code bases that were difficult to manage. We’ve all had the experience of getting an opaque number from a data partner and asking, “Can you help me trace this back to the source?” and finding that incredibly difficult.

When I joined dbt, the company had very little revenue — I think below $15 million in ARR — but there were already tens of thousands of companies using the open-source product. That told me the company was doing something special that really resonated with data developers. Since then, the platform has evolved into something much more robust that helps organizations govern data cross-platform at scale. In a world where CIOs and chief data officers are deeply focused on ensuring data quality doesn’t become a barrier to AI adoption, that’s become an increasingly important area of infrastructure.
CFOTL: Can we ask about the merger? I know there was a major announcement last year.
Riley: Last October, dbt signed a definitive agreement to merge with Fivetran, and we’re deeply excited about it. DBT and Fivetran have both become best-of-breed midsize players in the data platform space, and together the combined company becomes the third-largest standalone data platform company in the world behind Databricks and Snowflake.
It’s been a fascinating transaction to work on because the companies share so much common ground. Both organizations grew up at roughly the same time and both have very similar philosophies around being platform agnostic and supporting the user. It really felt like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to bring together two companies with such strong alignment.
CFOTL: Tell us something about your mindset when it comes to performance and what really drives performance in this business.
Riley: In addition to managing finance and accounting, I also manage our data team, so we spend a lot of time thinking about how to leverage our platform to create a truly data-driven environment internally. We’re very focused on product analytics, go-to-market analytics, and having absolute clarity around the KPIs that matter across every area of the business.
We invest early in building strong data literacy and accountability among our executives so that when we review financials, we’re reviewing them in tandem with business KPIs. Everyone understands that the investments we make are intended to drive specific outcomes. Every couple of quarters we revisit those assumptions to make sure we’re still focused on the right things. It’s really a hand-in-hand finance and data effort.
CFOTL: Before the results show up, what inputs matter most?
Riley: For us, the business KPIs are really the leading indicators. We focus heavily on the health and growth of our open-source community because that effectively becomes the top of our funnel. We’re constantly evaluating how customers are using new features, how that drives adoption of the platform product, and how we can make the experience even more compelling.
That thinking flows into our go-to-market planning as well. Do we have the right sellers? Do we have the right resources allocated? Do we have the right “chess pieces” on the board to hit our goals? Then we reflect back and ask whether those assumptions produced the financial profile we expected.
CFOTL: Can you share a little more about your insight into the customer experience and your efforts to understand it?
Riley: We try to be thoughtful about customer privacy, especially on the open-source side, so we don’t collect an excessive amount of data there. But we absolutely monitor feature consumption among customers who move onto the platform. We want to understand what they find valuable and what drives conversion.
For many open-source companies, the community is viewed primarily as a way to drive adoption or contribute to the engineering ecosystem. But from a finance perspective, I think you have to think about open source fundamentally as a distribution method. Our North Star is making sure that the commercial platform is valuable enough that it becomes an obvious next step for users. DBT’s open-source community is still growing about 70% year-over-year at scale, with more than 100,000 companies on the platform, so the opportunity is significant.

So long, dbt Labs, and thanks for all the fish
About three and a half years ago, I wrote an article about my career investment thesis on dbt Labs, and now nearly four years after joining, I find myself at the end of one journey and the beginning of a new adventure. It’s been an opportunity for reflection for myself, on why I joined, on what I learned, on how we evolved as an organization. Even as I move on from dbt Labs, I find myself still convicted on the product and the opportunity for dbt Labs.
If you haven’t subscribed yet, you can get thoughts and musings about personal finance and whatever else I find interesting straight to your inbox by clicking here:
The rise of the multi-platform enterprise
The most widely played marketing messages from Snowflake and Databricks these days center around AI, but if there was any one topic that rang out even louder at their annual conferences this past year, it was the table format war that had been going on for some time between Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Hudi. Databricks reportedly spent $2B to buy a small startup called Tabular that was productizing Iceberg for the enterprise.
Why? The answer is portability. Iceberg solves multiple problems all at once. For Snowflake customers, it’s a major cost improvement. Instead of storing raw datasets on S3, and then getting double charged for data storage after loading data into Snowflake, customers are able to query on top of Iceberg tables directly. Effectively, this reduces storage costs, without loss of efficacy at the query/BI layer. For both Snowflake and Databricks customers, this is a portability enhancer. Databricks customers can have flexibility by moving away from Delta Lake, which is open, but very Databricks platform-specific, and it enables both Databricks and Snowflake to operate as query layers on top of the Iceberg storage substrate, rather than having a fully integrated, and tightly coupled, stack.
For dbt, this has a couple major knock-on effects:
1. Companies will be much more inclined to use the right tool for the right job: have a use case that demands Snowflake? Query from Iceberg tables. Have a use case that demands Databricks? Query from your Iceberg lakehouse. Have a use case that demands streaming? Flink on top of Iceberg becomes an option.
2. Companies will be able to use the tool that is the cheapest for the job: Different processing systems will have different costs based on use cases, processing patterns, etc. By leaning into technologies that can work cross-platform, the business gains optionality and cost efficiencies by leveraging the lowest cost platform for the task at hand. You can imagine a future where you have a system that evaluates the cost of a job at runtime, and chooses the right platform based on current system load, etc.
In both of these scenarios, it’s absolutely critical to be bought into a platform that is agnostic to the underlying processing systems, and that’s where dbt Labs sits today. The recent SDF Labs acquisition provides some good insight into future strategy – SDF, at its core, is largely compiler technology that provides very sophisticated transpilation capabilities. It enables a dbt project to seamlessly move from one data platform to another, without requiring code rewrites or complex Jinja work (i.e. use of cross-database macros) to ensure that a model can execute in a cross-platform way. This is efficiency-enabling technology – it creates the pathway for dbt Labs to provide the ability for businesses to realize these benefits.
AI is not going away – governance and data quality are paramount
I worked for Cloudera over a decade ago, and one of the tag lines we were spouting in the early 2010s was “data is the new oil.” While the big data craze has meaningfully come and gone, as we enter a new era of AI, data is more than just oil to be drilled. It’s the whole damn moat. Increasingly, GenAI is creating a dynamic where massive companies can rise and fall overnight, and with foundation models proliferating at breakneck pace, the things that are meaningfully creating differentiation for this new crop of startups are the datasets themselves.
In order to effectively engineer an AI application, depending on whether you’re doing instruction tuning, fine-tuning, or leaning on RAG to produce a high quality experience, you need a well-curated dataset to drive the training and inference processes. Ensuring that data is consistently and accurately labeled, that it’s governed effectively, tooling like dbt ends up being a must-have in the data refinement process to drive data quality initiatives. It helps that products like Snowflake Cortex make all of this accessible directly through a SQL interface that dbt excels at integrating with.
Thinking about the potential boogeymen hiding in the data pipelines, the other thing that AI brings with it is rampant PII (and PHI and PCI and all of the other PXI) challenges. This is another arena where SDF will bring some interesting new capabilities to the fold. Specifically, SDF provides classifier primitives that will enable dbt to meaningfully trace lineage of PII through layers of transformation and data refinement. Being able to identify where PII lives is going to be critical for enterprises to maintain compliance, especially as regulation surrounding GenAI is inevitably ramped up over time. dbt is, again, laying the groundwork to be an impact player in the rapidly evolving world.
dbt has has staying power within the transformation market
An actual screenshot of dbt Labs’ internal Hex dashboards of revenue growth
Four years ago, when I joined, dbt had less than $5M in ARR. The company recently announced it had crossed the $100M milestone. While this isn’t the growth curve we’re seeing with some of the new AI upstarts, this remains an extremely fast approach to $100M, and it comes with a 5000-strong customer list. dbt clearly struck a chord with the data world, and has rapidly become a standard for data transformation across the industry. This can be seen by the sheer number of dbt execution platforms that exist these days. There are a myriad of companies that tout their ability to execute dbt code or have compatibility with dbt, not to mention companies like Databricks offering those capabilities integrated tightly with their existing data warehousing product. While this does produce an inherent level of competition, dbt Labs is accustomed to that due to the nature of the open-source model, and continues to be (certainly in my mind) the best place to go for a dbt-centric development platform.
One thing that didn’t meaningfully exist when I started at dbt Labs was competition. There were very few natural competitors beyond dbt Core, itself, and I called out that very apparent fact through the proxy of industry market maps. This is less true today, and I think that that underscores the standardization around dbt. Small upstarts like Paradime and Tobiko Data take different approaches to tackling dbt Labs as competition – Paradime is largely a runner of dbt Code, and Tobiko Data offers SQLMesh, which is a meaningfully different framework that takes a great deal of inspiration from dbt, and aims to provide zero-code-changes-required execution of dbt projects. In fact, Tobiko’s entire approach to the market seems to be to mirror every move that dbt Labs makes (as evidenced, for example, by their recent seemingly-shotgun-wedding of a Quarry acquihire, which I admittedly think is a more foolish approach than focusing on relentlessly solving customer problems). Larger startups like Coalesce.io have taken a more differentiated tack, but still display significant inspiration from dbt’s roots. Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.
Looking at larger scale competitors, the inevitable markets to look at are Informatica and Alteryx. Alteryx was taken private in a $4.4B deal, which can only be taken to indicate that they’ve had a challenging time shifting their energy away from their historical desktop app-based interface, and likely indicates that their cloud strategy (predominantly the acquisition of Trifacta) has fallen flat. Similarly, Informatica is on a years-long journey to migrate their perpetual license-based revenue from PowerCenter to subscription-based recurring revenue with their Informatica Intelligence Cloud Services product, and while they have the benefit of a massive amount of revenue, their stock plummeted 25% last month when their cloud renewals fell short of Street expectations. These are meaningful chinks in the armor of historical giants, and $10B+ of TAM at play – from my vantage point, this is strictly opportunity for dbt Labs.
Lastly on the topic, it’s important to look at the partnership angle. dbt Labs has historically had a very strong attachment to Snowflake and other platforms (Redshift, BigQuery, and the like) that look more like traditional data warehouses than newer-age lakehouses. This, too, is an opportunity. The implication is that Databricks, which is seeing blazingly fast adoption, is a rising tide that will inevitably lift dbt Labs’ boat. Databricks’ CRO, Ron Gabrisko, was a recent attendee and speaker at the dbt Labs Sales Kick-off, and it’s reasonable to expect an energetic partner motion headed forward. This happens to coincide with an interesting little announcement from the Databricks SKO that they had acquired Bladebridge, which is a technology-backed consultancy that focuses on platform migration projects. This mirrors Snowflake’s acquisition of Mobilize.net (who developed a tool called SnowConvert) from a couple years ago. However, where Snowflake’s primary target was very clearly Teradata, Databricks’ target is aimed directly at the jugular of Snowflake. The fallout of the Snowflake and Databricks war all benefits platforms that aim towards agnosticism, and I feel strongly that dbt Labs will be a beneficiary.
“It’s the people, stupid”
The last major tailwind I see for dbt Labs today is the people. dbt Labs has long employed some of the smartest, most talented people I’ve had the pleasure to work alongside in my career. However, in recent days, the theme has clearly been on upleveling the executive ranks. As an aside, I’m married to a highly-talented woman (the far more impressive half of the couple) who recruits for CROs and a variety of GTM leaders for venture-backed startups. One of the things I’ve learned seeing her practice her craft is the importance of matching the executive to the growth phase. There are various inflection points for companies as revenue scales, and as dbt Labs is existing the $0-100M phase, and entering the $100-500M phase, the company is staffing up with people have seen the proverbial movie before, and will be able to help the company navigate the next several years. For example:
 Sarah Riley (CFO) helped Okta and Zoom chart their paths through IPO
 Brandon Sweeney (COO) was at the helm of HashiCorp from their $100-$500M IPO run
 Austin Stefani (CRO) led Rubrik’s Americas org to a successful IPO outcome
 Ryan Segar (CCO) previously led Sisense’s technical field organization through their rise
 Mark Porter (CTO) was GM for several major AWS services, and most recently CTO of MongoDB
 Sally Jenkins (CMO) is in her fourth stint as CMO, having previously done the job at Informatica and Elastic (among others)
This is an absolutely stacked set of executives (even ignoring the extremely talented set of people operating at VP and other executive levels), and is exactly the type of group that I would hope to see at an IPO hopeful.
Acknowledging my biases
This all stated, I still have immense bias here. I have a lot of shares sitting in Carta, and desperately want to realize a large amount of value from those down the road. The inevitable question is: can dbt Labs go the distance?
It’s impossible for me to be sure of the outcome, but I feel confident that dbt Labs is on the path to success. And what I can definitively say is that I’m incredibly proud of what the team at dbt Labs has built, and so grateful to have been a part of the story.
So why did I leave? Stay tuned for the answer to that one.

Sarah Jane Friar OBE (born 24 December 1972) is a British-Irish and American business executive, who has been the chief financial officer (CFO) of OpenAI since June 2024. She was the chief executive officer of American technology company Nextdoor from 2018 to 2024 and the CFO of Block, Inc. (formerly Square, Inc.) from 2012 to 2018.
Early life
[edit]
[personal detail removed]eland. She attended Strabane Grammar School. Friar won a scholarship from the accounting firm Arthur Andersen after entering a competition; she then worked there for a year before pursuing engineering studies at University of Oxford. She studied metallurgy, economics, and management at Oxford, and then completed an MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business where she was an Arjay Miller scholar. Friar interned at Ashanti Goldfields in 1990s, during which she was assigned to work at a gold mine in Ghana.
Career
[edit]
Friar worked as an analyst for McKinsey & Company in South Africa, a managing director in equity research at Goldman Sachs, and a senior vice president of finance and strategy at Salesforce before becoming chief financial officer at Square in 2012. She then joined Nextdoor, a hyperlocal social networking service for neighborhoods, as CEO in 2018. Friar led the company public through a special-purpose acquisition company in 2021. Nextdoor announced Friar would step down as CEO in mid-2024. In June 2024, she joined OpenAI, the artificial intelligence research organization that develops ChatGPT, as its first CFO.
Friar is on the boards of Walmart and ConsenSys, and previously sat on the boards of Slack Technologies and New Relic's boards. She also co-chairs Stanford's Digital Economy Lab and runs Ladies Who Launch, a non-profit focused on female entrepreneurs that she co-founded.
She received an honorary doctorate from Ulster University in 2018. In 2019, she was granted an Order of the British Empire from Queen Elizabeth II for her commitment to entrepreneurship and financial services.
Personal life
[edit]
Friar is married to David Riley, a former hedge fund partner. The couple has a daughter and son. She lives in Marin County, California. She was also named on Time "Time (magazine)")'s list of the most influential people in the world in 2026.

Square CFO Sarah Friar steps down to join Nextdoor as CEO
By Selina WangUpdated
Mac Riley, center, son of Square CFO Sarah Friar, rings a ceremonial bell as the Square IPO begins trading, on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2015. Flanking Riley are Square CEO Jack Dorsey, left, and co-founder Jim McKelvey, far right. Square, the 6-year-old startup known for its white, cube-shaped card readers that plug into smartphones, is surging in its first day as a publicly traded company. (AP Photo/Richard Drew)
Richard Drew / Associated Press 2015
Nextdoor CEO and co-founder Nirav Tolia, on Wed. Aug. 24, 2016, at their headquarters in San Francisco, California, explains the changes the company has made to their social network after accusations of racial profiling surfaced from the community.
Michael Macor / The Chronicle 2016
Sarah Friar, the chief financial officer of Square, is leaving the electronic payments company to become chief executive officer of Nextdoor, a social network for local neighborhoods. Square shares declined as much as 9 percent in extended trading Wednesday.
David Viniar, Square’s lead independent director and a former Goldman Sachs financial chief, will lead the search for Friar’s successor, the San Francisco company said. Friar will stay at Square into December. Nextdoor is also headquartered in San Francisco.
A longtime Goldman Sachs analyst, Friar joined Square as CFO in 2012 when she was an executive at Salesforce.com. Her hiring received applause from analysts and investors, who saw her as a driver of growth and stability at Square, whose CEO, Jack Dorsey, serves in the same role at Twitter. The company, which held its initial public offering in November 2015, has more than doubled in value over the past year as it topped Wall Street estimates.

Nextdoor raised $75 million in December at a $1.5 billion valuation, according to Pitchbook Data. Nirav Tolia, co-founder and CEO of Nextdoor, announced in July that he would step down from the executive post.
“Nextdoor is one of those rare companies that transcends its utility as a business and is quickly making its mark on communities here and around the world,” Friar said in a statement announcing her appointment as CEO.

It has expanded into loans, food delivery, instant deposits, accounting, inventory, website building and more. WHEELING, W.V. (WTRF) — A couple accused of hiding remains of a missing man appeared in Ohio County Circuit Court Monday.
Christopher and Sarah Riley pleaded guilty to the felony offense of concealment of a deceased human body.
In 2021, human remains were found in Ohio County that were identified as Andrew Downs.
Two years later the Ohio County Sheriff’s Office received information that Downs had died and was buried behind Leopold Lane in Wheeling.
In 2025 the Riley’s turned themselves in.
Ohio County prosecuting attorney Shawn Turak says she suspects the cause of death was likely linked to drug use.
“Instead of contacting police, 911, they buried the body in backyard in Ohio County at the residence they were living in at the time, and they were living with Mr. Downs at the time. There’s a plethora of drug activity involved in this case and it leads to common sense that that was most likely the cause of death of Andrew Downs.”
Shawn Turak, Ohio County prosecuting attorney
In the coming weeks, Turak says there will be a pre-sentence investigation report followed by a sentencing hearing.
Turak says the couple could face one to five years of incarceration.

Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'

Getty A woman with long dark hair wearing a black jacket gestures with her hands
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

by Laura Varley
4 Nov 2026
Wooden pegs representing people standing outside wooden blocks with plus and minus signs.
Image: © VRVIRUS/Stock.adobe.com
The changes are expected to impact around 22pc of the organisation’s workforce and are in response to a recent dip in the company’s growth.
Canva, the graphic design company, has announced plans to significantly restructure its current workforce. The organisation, which is based in Sydney, Australia, reported a slow-down in its growth for the first time in a decade. 1,271 jobs, around 22pc, are expected to be affected by the restructuring and cuts. 
In a message sent to Canva’s staff on Tuesday (3 November), Melanie Perkins, the group’s co-founder and CEO said, “Today, I have some profoundly difficult news to share. 
“After months of thinking through how to set Canva up for the next chapter, we have made the incredibly hard decision to make significant changes to how we’re organised, where some of our teams are based and the roles and skills we need for the future.”
She explained that the change in the company’s structure will mean some employees will see their roles changed or will be relocated to centralised hubs, while others will have their roles eliminated. 
She said, “This is without doubt the hardest moment in our 13 year history. Behind every decision is someone we care deeply about and I know the consequences will be very real for those directly affected, their families, friends and teammates.”
As part of the next steps, among other benefits, those affected will receive a minimum of six months salary, the one-year vesting restrictions will be removed for employees who joined in the last year, there will be 12 months of continued healthcare coverage and career support while employees navigate the changes. 
Moving forward, Canva stated that Sydney will become the primary home for more of its product teams and for roles in other specialities where collaboration is necessary. From the start of the new year, January 2027, there will also be a push to get hybrid employees back into the office, two to three days a week. 
Canva announced their plans for restructuring in a landscape where many organisations are having to make tough decisions. 
Virgin Media O2 recently said it is laying off thousands of employees in a cost-cutting drive as it looks to tackle its £22bn debt. 
File storage platform Dropbox is laying off around 200 people, or 9pc of its global workforce, across engineering, product, design and administrative functions.
And banking and financial services company Barclays expects to cut 5,000 jobs as part of a wider plan to cut costs using artificial intelligence.

Introducing Canva Grow 2.0: Create, launch, and learn from ads, all in one place
Today at Cannes Lions, we unveiled Canva Grow 2.0, and with it, a new way for marketing teams to create, launch, and learn from ads – all without leaving Canva.
Empowering the world to design has always been at the heart of Canva, and for businesses of all sizes, that's always meant more than making things look good. For marketing teams, it's meant finding new ways to help them move faster, do more with less, and create work that actually drives results. But for all the ground we've covered, one problem kept coming up: the tools for creating ads, publishing them, and understanding how they performed were always separate, leaving teams to stitch together their own workflow across platforms and start each new campaign largely from scratch.
Today, at the Canva Creative Cabana during the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity, we unveiled Canva Grow 2.0. Designed to help teams stop managing tools and start building better campaigns, Canva Grow 2.0 brings ad creation, publishing, and performance optimization into a single AI-native workflow – and it's the most significant launch we've made for marketing teams yet.
The problem we set out to solve
The modern ad workflow is broken in a way that most marketing teams have simply learned to live with. Creative lives in one tool, publishing happens in another, and performance data sits somewhere else entirely, leaving teams with slower campaigns, siloed work, and insights that rarely find their way back into the next round of creative.
At the same time, content demands have never been more intense. Ads burn out in two to four weeks, platforms like Meta and TikTok are hungry for 50 or more variants at a time, and most teams simply can't produce content fast enough to keep pace. Even when they can, they're spending hours on the logistics of running a campaign rather than the thinking and creative work that actually moves the needle.
Canva Grow 2.0 is built specifically for that reality, closing the loop between creation and performance so teams can generate ads with AI, publish them across platforms, learn from real-time data, and automatically refresh what isn't working. Every campaign becomes a feedback loop, and every iteration builds on what came before.
Ads built to convert
The foundation of Canva Grow 2.0 is a significantly upgraded AI-powered ad creation experience that removes the specialist resource and production time that effective ad creation has historically demanded. Drop in your website and Canva Grow pulls in your business information, product visuals, brand colors, and audience signals to generate high-performing static and video ads in moments – all ready to customize and launch.
Canva Grow Ad Creation
Canva Grow Ad Creation
The AI is doing more than generating pretty creative here. It ingests your brand context and what's already performing in your account to build ads designed for conversion from the start, whether you're creating something new or generating fresh concepts based on your best-performing work. And with the new Magic Layers⁠(opens in a new tab or window) integration, any AI-generated ad can be exported directly into the Canva editor for further refinement, so you get the speed of AI generation without giving up the creative control that makes your work distinctly yours.
One place to publish everywhere
Historically, getting ads live has been its own project: a process of exporting files, logging into multiple ad managers, and manually recreating campaign settings across platforms. Canva Grow 2.0 replaces all of that with a single unified publishing workflow, letting you push ads directly from Canva across Meta, TikTok, and LinkedIn, regardless of whether those ads were created in Canva Grow, designed in the Canva editor, or uploaded from another source.
Canva Grow Ad Publishing
Canva Grow Ad Publishing
The new Launch Dashboard sits alongside Bulk Publish to give you a centralized view of every campaign running across all three platforms at once, so instead of switching between ad managers to understand what's live and what's performing, you can oversee, manage, and adjust your entire paid media mix without ever leaving Canva.
Smart defaults handle the manual setup work that usually slows teams down between creation and going live, turning what used to mean multiple exports, multiple logins, and a lot of copy-pasting into one seamless flow.
From performance data to your next best ad
The real step-change in Canva Grow 2.0 is what happens after your ads go live, because understanding performance and acting on it has always been the hardest part of the loop to close. Multi-Platform Ad Insights & Reports brings performance reporting into a single visual experience where you can identify top-performing creative, spot trends across campaigns, build custom reports, and share insights across your team without bouncing between platforms.
Canva Grow Ad Insights
Canva Grow Ad Insights
What makes this experience genuinely different is the AI that sits underneath it. AI Ad Tagging automatically analyzes and labels every ad with structured tags, surfacing the themes, formats, messages, and creative elements that are actually driving results across large ad sets – analysis that used to take a strategist hours to pull together now happens the moment your campaigns sync. And with directional coaching built into the dashboard, you're never left staring at data without knowing what to do with it – it tells you not just which ads are working, but why, and what to make more of.
Automatic Refresh Generation brings the whole loop full circle. When you open Canva Grow, you'll find a pipeline of fresh ad concepts and variations already waiting, generated based on what's actually performing in your Meta account rather than built from scratch, so every new campaign starts from a stronger foundation than the last.
The foundation for what comes next
For us, this is the beginning of something bigger. We've been making accelerated strategic investments in AI⁠(opens in a new tab or window) and marketing technology⁠(opens in a new tab or window), and Canva Grow is where that starts to come together into something teams can use every day. Because for businesses of all sizes, we're committed to becoming a genuine end-to-end marketing system: one where creative and performance work together, and where the learnings from every campaign feed directly into the next one.
Creative and performance have been separated for too long. Canva Grow 2.0 is how we start to close that gap, and we're just getting started. To learn more, visit canva.com/canva-grow⁠(opens in a new tab or window).

Canva hosted 60+ interns in a single recent cohort, all working on a product used by 260 million monthly active users, and it fills those seats in a 30-day window. For the 2027–2028 cycle, the ANZ summer program (December 2027 start) is expected to open applications around April 2027, while US summer roles (May–August 2028) typically post September through November. That 30-day ANZ window isn't a suggestion: Prosple’s listing documented a late-April open and late-May close for the last cycle, and Reddit users report that positions close when filled, not when the calendar says so.
What Is a Canva Internship?
A Canva internship is a paid, 12-week summer placement that puts penultimate-year students into real product teams at one of the world’s largest private tech companies, valued at $42–65 billion. Interns ship features used by 260 million monthly active users across design, engineering, data, and marketing tracks. The program starts with a one-week onboarding bootcamp and is remote-friendly: "if you want to do work from the office, at home, or a bit of both, it’s completely up to you." Glassdoor rates Canva 3.9 out of 5 from 862 reviews, with intern interviews scoring a 67% positive experience rate. The 37 former interns who transitioned to full-time through Canva’s Launchpad program show the pipeline is real.
When Do Canva Internship Applications Open for 2027–2028?
Canva’s calendar splits across two hemispheres, and the distinction matters more than most applicants realize. The ANZ summer program (December start) opens applications around April, keeps the window live for roughly 30 days, and closes by late May. The US summer program (May–August) posts roles September through November on a rolling basis. For the 2027–2028 cycle, that means the ANZ window is expected around April–May 2027 (about 8 months before the December start), while US roles should appear September–November 2027. The overall interview process runs 4–5 weeks from recruiter call to decision, which is fast by tech standards. One thing to note: Canva has not posted 2027–2028 dates yet, so registering interest via their Early Careers page is the only way to catch the window when it opens.

Why You Must Apply the Week Applications Open
Canva’s official Early Careers page says the internship is a 12-week program for penultimate-year students, and Prosple’s listing documented that "roles will be live for 30 days." Thirty days is the entire window, and review is rolling inside it. Reddit confirms the pattern: one thread notes that applications were still being accepted in mid-May for a recent intake, with the board closing shortly after. Another thread asks if anyone even got the OA, and the answer was mostly rejections. The math is simple: a 30-day window with rolling review means late applicants compete for whatever seats the first two weeks didn’t fill.

Seven confirmed internship tracks span engineering, design, data, and business. Which one should you pick? The honest answer is the one whose skills you can already show, because each track interviews against its own technical bar. And one common thread runs through all of them: product thinking, the ability to connect your work to outcomes for 260 million users.

What Are the Eligibility Requirements?
Canva publishes the same core requirements across its internship tracks:
• Enrollment: penultimate-year (second-to-last year) tertiary student. Canva’s official early careers page says the program is for "penultimate year tertiary students," and FinalRoundAI reports expected graduation dates of Dec 2026 to Jun 2028 for the current cycle.
• Degree fields: CS, Design, Statistics, or closely related disciplines for engineering and design tracks. Marketing and other tracks have their own requirements.
• Work authorization: Australian work rights required for Sydney and Melbourne roles. US work authorization preferred for Austin and San Francisco. No explicit visa sponsorship language found in any posting.
• Availability: the full 12 weeks. The program is remote-friendly: "if you want to do work from the office, at home, or a bit of both, it’s completely up to you."
Does Canva Have a GPA Cutoff?
No. No GPA requirement appears in any Canva internship posting, FAQ, or careers page. This is verified absence, not omission: Canva’s official how-we-hire page emphasizes skills and product thinking over academic scores, and explicitly says "even if you don’t think you quite meet all of the skills listed or tick all the boxes, we’d still love to hear from you." What actually gates you? Two things. The penultimate-year requirement excludes graduating seniors and first-year students alike. And work-authorization requirements vary by office: Australian work rights for Sydney/Melbourne, US authorization for Austin/SF. Beyond that, Canva screens for product-building experience, technical skills, and alignment with its "Crazy Big Goals" culture.

What Is the Canva Application and Interview Process Like?
Canva’s funnel is structured and runs about 4–5 weeks from recruiter call to decision:
1. Apply at lifeatcanva.com with your resume. You’ll get a confirmation email immediately. About 1–2 weeks later, a recruiter reviews your application and, if successful, arranges a Zoom call.
2. Recruiter Zoom call (20–30 min). Aspirations, experience, and culture fit. Canva calls this the "initial conversation" and says it kicks off the 4–5 week process.
3. Online Assessment (90 min, 3 questions). For backend SWE, this is Java-only with no other language options. ML/AI adds math/stats-heavy MCQs. Reddit consensus: "Hardest part of Canva’s intern process is passing the OA."
4. Technical interview and offer. SWE: LeetCode easy/easy-medium plus system design. ML/AI: 75-minute final (15 min behavioral + 60 min technical coding, AI-assisted). Offers specify team, location, and compensation.
One thing that makes Canva’s process unusual: they explicitly encourage AI use at every stage, including interviews. "Just be ready to explain how you used it, what you kept, changed, or built on." The behavioral portion uses the STARR method (Situation, Task, Action, Results, Reflection), not standard STAR, so practice adding the Reflection step. Glassdoor rates intern interview difficulty 3 out of 5 with an average 22-day process.

How Do You Stand Out When 60 Seats Fill in 30 Days?
Three moves, all executable before April. First, apply in week one of the window. Rolling review plus positions that close when filled makes timing itself a filter. Second, build the evidence Canva actually evaluates: product-thinking projects, AI-assisted development workflow, and portfolio proof that you shipped something. Canva’s interviewers use the STARR method and explicitly ask how you use AI tools, so having a project where you used AI to build, tested the output, and iterated on it's worth more than another LeetCode solve. Third, prepare for the OA like it’s the real gate, because Reddit says it's. For backend, that means Java fluency (no language choice). For ML, it means brushing up on math and stats fundamentals alongside coding. The technical interview after the OA is reportedly easier. And remember what 37 Launchpad conversions tell you: the internship is a 12-week audition for a full-time role.

FAQ
When do Canva internship applications open for 2027–2028?
For the ANZ summer program (December 2027 start), applications typically open in April and stay live for about 30 days, closing in late May. For US summer roles (May–August 2028), postings appear September through November. Canva has not posted 2027–2028 dates yet, so register your interest at lifeatcanva.com/en/early-careers/ and check back early 2027.
Is Canva internship recruiting rolling?
Partially. The ANZ intake has a defined 30-day application window (typically April–May), while US roles reportedly recruit on a rolling basis from September. In both cases, positions close when filled, so applying early within the window gives you the best chance. Reddit users report high rejection rates even at the OA stage.
What GPA or grades do you need for a Canva internship?
Canva doesn't publish a minimum GPA requirement. Their official hiring page emphasizes skills, product thinking, and cultural alignment over academic scores. They explicitly encourage candidates to apply even if they don’t tick all the boxes. Focus on demonstrating product-building experience, technical skills, and alignment with Canva’s Crazy Big Goals culture.
What is the Canva interview process like?
For engineering interns, expect a 90-minute online assessment (3 coding questions, Java-only for backend), followed by a recruiter Zoom call, then a technical interview with LeetCode-style problems and system design. ML/AI adds math-heavy MCQs. The process takes about 4–5 weeks. Canva encourages using AI tools and asks you to explain how you used them.
Do Canva interns get return offers?
Return-offer rates vary significantly by year and market conditions. Third-party estimates put the normal rate around 60%, but during hiring freezes (like 2024–2025), the rate dropped as low as 11% with almost no external grad roles. Canva’s Launchpad program is the primary pipeline from internship to full-time. 37 former interns returned through Launchpad in one cohort.
What skills does Canva look for in interns?
Canva values product thinking across all tracks, the ability to connect technical work to user outcomes for 260 million monthly users. Engineers need Python or Java plus framework experience. ML roles need deep learning and PyTorch. Designers need a portfolio showing product and visual craft. All tracks are evaluated on AI literacy: how you use AI tools, what you kept, changed, or built on.
Are Canva internships paid?
Yes. Australian SWE interns earn approximately A$28–38 per hour (A$61K–79K annualized) with meals provided. US roles reportedly pay $46–60 per hour for SWE, with ML/AI trending higher at $52–60 per hour. US interns receive relocation assistance for Austin and San Francisco. Canva pays 18% above the Australian national average for SWE interns.
Is the Canva backend OA really Java-only?
Yes. Multiple Reddit reports confirm the backend SWE online assessment is Java-only with no other language options. This is a major differentiator versus most tech companies that allow language choice. The OA is 90 minutes for 3 questions at roughly medium difficulty. ML/AI OAs are different: math and stats heavy with both MCQs and coding, and language choice may vary.
The window is 30 days long and the review inside it's rolling. Spend the runway building proof: a remote Externship turns "interested in tech" into a finished AI or product project an April application can point at.

What is a balance sheet?
A balance sheet is a document that shows the financial health of a company at a specific point in time, usually at the end of every quarter or year. It lists all the business’s assets (resources owned) and liabilities (obligations owed) to determine the net assets or equity. Its name comes from its need to be “balanced,” meaning the total assets should equal the sum of the business’s liabilities and equity.
It's also called a statement of financial position, as it provides a snapshot of the company’s financial situation within a given reporting date, rather than its financial activities over time.
The balance sheet serves two purposes, depending on the person viewing the report. When viewed internally, it helps stakeholders gain clarity on whether the business is succeeding or not. It allows them to make necessary adjustments or focus on the positives. When viewed externally, it provides potential investors with insight into the business’s resources and its financial structure.
As a financial report, balance sheets are used across different industries and fields to aid decision-making and assess the overall financial health of an organization. It's not just limited to businesses, as personal balance sheet templates are a popular way to determine a person’s net worth.
For an easy-to-use balance sheet template, try Canva Sheets⁠(opens in a new tab or window). Create a custom financial report by entering the details of your assets and liabilities to calculate your equity.

Key components of a balance sheet
The balance sheet primarily focuses on this core equation:
assets = liabilities + equity
Based on this formula, a typical balance sheet format has three key components:
Assets
This is defined as anything a business or entity owns that holds value and can be converted to cash. It’s recorded as a positive (+) in a simple balance sheet template. An asset is further categorized into current and noncurrent assets.
Current assets are anything that a business expects to be converted into cash within a year. These can be cash and other cash equivalents, inventory, prepaid expenses, accounts receivable, and marketable securities.
Noncurrent assets are long-term investments that aren’t easily convertible to cash quickly, such as land, brands, trademarks, intellectual property, and equipment.
Liabilities
A liability is anything that a business owes to a third-party entity. It can be financial or legal obligations and is recorded as a negative (-) in a balance sheet template. A liability can also include an obligation to provide goods and services in the future. It's also further categorized as a current liability or a noncurrent liability.
A current liability includes anything due within a year. This can be payroll, rent, utilities, accounts payable, debt financing, and other accrued expenses.
Noncurrent liabilities are the long-term obligations that are not due within a year. These can be leases, bonds payable, loans, deferred tax liabilities, and provisions for pensions.
Equity
This is the last of the balance sheet elements. It’s also called owner’s equity or shareholders’ equity. It refers to the value remaining for owners after all the liabilities are accounted for. Equity typically consists of contributed capital and retained earnings.

Balance sheet FAQs
Why is a balance sheet important?
A balance sheet is important because it provides an essential snapshot of a business’s financial situation—assets, liabilities, and equity. This is crucial for assessing the overall financial health, liquidity, and solvency. The balance sheet is also a primary document for making informed financial decisions.
How to read a balance sheet?
Reading a balance sheet requires understanding its structure and the key balance sheet elements. You need to confirm its report date and that its fundamental equation holds in the report. It might also be necessary to assess the financial health by evaluating key balance sheet ratios and comparing the current report with previous ones.
What is the difference between a balance sheet and an income statement?
Although they're both key financial statements, the difference between a balance sheet and an income statement lies in their purpose. A balance sheet shows the financial position at a specific point in time. This tells you what the business owns and owes as of that specific date. Meanwhile, an income statement shows the business’s financial performance over a certain period. This tells you how much money the business has made or lost over a specified duration.

Aside from that, Canva Sheets make collaboration easy. Share Sheets with other teammates and work on your balance sheets together.
